utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Theunens. Can you hear me okay?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When we broke last night, you were discussing several examples of unified command between the JNA and local TO in particular localities that appear in the indictment. We're going to continue on that same topic for a few more minutes this morning. And to start, I'd like to ask you to look at document 65 ter number 1251. The B/C/S ERN of that document is 01527773. Just to remind everyone, we're around page 108, 109 in Mr. Theunens's report. Mr. Theunens, can you see that document on your screen now in English?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. This document is an order from the command of the 13th Corps - that is a JNA unit - as we can see from the heading in the left top corner. It is dated the 7th of November 1991, and on the last page, we can see the name of the commander of the unit, Colonel Slobodan Djordjevic. In the context of the topic we are discussing at the moment, I would like to draw attention to heading number 2, which is on the top of the second page. And in heading number 2, you can see that the corps commander or the commander orders that the sector of Saborsko, Funtana and Kuselj villages, there will be operations; i.e., the enemy forces will be destroyed, and then once that is done, the area will be overtaken by forces of the TO of Plaski and Titovo Korenica, which are units of the SAO Krajina Territorial Defence. The TO Titovo Korenica is also mentioned a bit downwards on the same page. We can see it in the heading 3. So again this shows single command between JNA and TO whereby the TO is subordinated to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this document be given an exhibit number and be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 52, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The next document is 65 ter number 1249; the ERN in B/C/S is 01527793 to 7795. Mr. Theunens, I've taken this one slightly out of chronological order, I apologise for that. Could you please tell us what this document is and point out any relevant passages.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is an order from the commander of the 1st Battalion of the SAO Krajina Plaski TO. We can see that again from the heading in the left top corner. This document is related to the previous document. All these documents deal with operations in the Saborsko area. Here we have a TO order. Interesting passage is under the heading 2, which starts at the bottom of the page. Information about our forces. May we go then to the top of the next page? So this is on the top of the second page of the order, that's a continuation of the heading 2, information about our forces. There it is mentioned that the 1st Battalion of the Plascanska TO Brigade has been reinforced with forces from the unit for special purposes, police reserve forces, and military police. Now, unit for special purposes, then we think or this is the unit of the SAO Krajina special purpose police, police reserve is also pretty obvious, and military police can include TO or JNA. So this document shows that in this case, TO and police operate together whereby TO SAO Krajina unit has been reinforced with elements of the SAO Krajina Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this receive a number and be admitted please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 53, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The next document is 65 ter number 1253. The ERN in B/C/S is 02029343 to 9344. Mr. Theunens, please look at this document and tell us what it is and point us to the significant passages.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an order from the 5th Military District command from the JNA, signed, as you can see on the second page at the bottom, by Colonel General Zivota Avramovic, and it is an order to form the 3rd Operations Group. Interesting passage here is the heading 2, which is on the bottom of the first page, where it is mentioned -- where it is described which units are subordinated to the 3rd Operational Group, and you will see that there are JNA units and SAO Krajina TO units among the units that are subordinated to the 3rd Operational Group or among the units that are part of the 3rd Operational Group, which is in line with the doctrinal issues we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If this could receive a number and be admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 54, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I have two additional documents on, I think, the same theme, so perhaps if you can just look at them and if they just reinforce what you said earlier, you can say that and we can go through them a little more quickly. The first one is 65 ter number 1265; the B/C/S ERN is 02032589 to 2591.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. This is just a confirmation of what we discussed earlier. When we scroll down on the first page to the middle of the page, we will see -- you will see that explicitly it is mentioned -- it is explicitly mentioned that all units in the area are placed under the single command of OG 3; i.e., the highest JNA command in the area of responsibility of the subordinate units and formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just please remind us what "OG" stands for.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "OG" stands for "Operational Group."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this receive a number and be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is received into evidence, and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 55, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The final document with regard to Saborsko is 65 ter number 1858. B/C/S ERN is 02032584 to 2586. Mr. Theunens, if you could again have a look at that and tell us whether or not it supports what you've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we look in the document at the headings 2 and 3, so at the bottom of the first page, the document in the head -- under the heading 2 details or states that in addition to JNA units there are also a number of Territorial Defence units that are placed under the command of the tactical group number 2, and these units are identified. And in the heading 3, under the heading 3, the task of tactical group number 2, in accordance with this particular order, is described.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If this could also receive a number and be admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, and may it please be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 56, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, staying on the same topic of joint command but changing localities, I'd like you to look at document 65 ter number 2059. The B/C/S ERN is 02015502. It's just one page.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an order from the 2nd and 3rd operational zone headquarters for Banja and Kordun. This operational zone headquarters refers to the SAO Krajina Territorial Defence. Earlier in the document when we discussed the establishment of a TO SAO Krajina staff, the operational zone structure is detailed. This is an order on cooperation with JNA units, and it specifies then the missions under the heading 2 and 3, the missions of a number of TO SAO Krajina units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Mr. Theunens: You said earlier in the document, when we discussed the establishment of the SAO Krajina TO staff, was that a -- did you mean earlier in your report or earlier in this document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier in my report, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this receive a number and be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted evidence, and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 57, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The final document on this topic is 65 ter number 173. The B/C/S ERN is 02011628.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an order from the command of the 1st Operational Group, so a JNA command, and in the second paragraph of the document, the commander, Major General Spiro Ninkovic explicitly states that all Territorial Defence units in his zone of responsibility or in the zone of operations of the 1st Operational Group are placed under the command of the 1st Operational Group starting from the date mentioned in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could it receive a number and be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, can we just see the top address on the document. Mr. Theunens, what is the Socialist Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was the structure or that was the name of Croatia before it became independent from the SFRY, and I believe that actually the unit -- the stamp is from the receiver and that the receiver used this stamp. On one hand he state that they are part of the Socialist Republic of Croatia, but on the other hand when we look then at the situation at that time, the municipality of Vojnic is part of the territory controlled by the entity known as the SAO Krajina TO -- SAO Krajina. So there is a bit of a contradiction because, as you pointed out, this would -- the stamp would indicate that this is a unit that is part of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia, but when we look at the date, 20th of October, and we also take the document into context with other documents, my analysis would be, or is, that at that time this TO unit is actually not responding any more to the Republic of Croatia but to the SAO Krajina. So the stamp, from that point of view, would be misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm misled by the apparent source of the document, given the address of the author.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The stamp, Your Honour, on the right top corner is actually a stamp of a receiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see the stamp, unless the stamp is at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the B/C/S copy, which is -- you can't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm looking at the English copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Would it be possible for the Court officer to show the B/C/S on the monitor so we could have a better view of this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, as this is our first run through a bunch of documents with e-court, I'm not sure what we can do and what we can't do, but I think we ought to be able to see this in B/C/S on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can always ask Judge Hoepfel to help us. He's got --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Here we go, Your Honour, it's come up on the screen now. At the top of that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That makes better sense. This is the stamp of the receiver. It's not the address of the author.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Theunens, the way the Chamber has stated it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, when taking into account or assuming that this document is established according to the rules for the drafting of orders and reports that were -- that applied to the JNA, the author of the document, or let's say the command that is issuing the order, is always identified on the left top corner, and then the stamp of the receiver can be put anywhere. Now, here it is put on the right top side. It could also -- quite often when we have documents, the stamp of the receiver is put at the left -- in the left bottom corner, where also the time is mentioned and also a number is given to register the document as an incoming order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Theunens. That original document at least clears the question in my mind. Thank you, you may proceed, Mr. Black. You asked if it may be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 58, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, from pages 112 to 118 of your report, which are pages 133 to 139 in B/C/S, you discuss some documents which you say "indicate that there were problems with the maintaining of discipline and the prevention of crime during the operations in Croatia." Now, first, could you please summarise how these documents indicate that there were problems maintaining discipline and preventing crimes among members of the TO.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the documents that have been discussed in page 112 to 118 of my report consist of orders by senior JNA officers where they warn their subordinates, and in particular TO, to abide by military discipline and also military -- and the rules of -- the laws of war. And also I've quoted from a number of investigations that were carried out by security -- people called security organs, so members of the security service within the SFRY armed forces, who have been informed that in certain areas alleged violations of the laws and customs of war have taken place and who drafted reports on these alleged violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, let me take you to one document in particular, which you reproduced in large part on pages 114 to 117. The 65 ter number is 2041, and the ERN is 04192153 to 2156. If possible, could we have the English shown on the screen again as we were before. Thank you. Mr. Theunens, would you look at this document, please, and tell us what it is and what it shows us.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an order by the command of the 9th JNA Corps, also known as the Knin Corps; Colonel Vukovic. An order he issued on the 20th of October which is called combatting the crime in the zone of combat activities of the 9th Corps. The copy we have here is the one that was addressed to the command of the 1st TO Partizan Brigade. And in this order, Vukovic gives instructions on what should we do to maintain discipline and also prevent crimes. He specifies the crimes that have taken place, and he also mentions what should be done to prevent or to act against crimes. In that context, I would like to draw your attention to the last part of the heading 2, which is mentioned on the beginning of the second page. Colonel Vukovic there states that in taking measures for the protection of citizens and property, the armed forces or all elements of the armed forces have to cooperate with the legal organs of the government, particularly the organs of security, and they should then take the measures within their jurisdiction. This indicates that at that time there are bodies of government in the zone of responsibility in the 9th Corps, so local government, and there are also organs or structures that are able to maintain security and law and order outside the military. In normal circumstances, when the military is operating somewhere, you don't expect civilians to be there and the military police will take care of law and order in first instance, but this passage indicates that in the zone of responsibility of the 9th Corps, as I mentioned, there is a civilian authority and also structures under that civilian authority which can maintain law and order and also act against crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this receive a number and be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question. How, then, does the intermingling between the civil security authority and the military authority interact with the concept of uniform command control within the army? It seems to be contradicting what we have been told earlier, that there was single command and the command would be within the army structure. Now there seems now to be also some authority coming from the civil society.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the principle of single and unified command and also the third principle obligation to implement decisions, applied to military operations, and military operations - for example, an attack - will start with an order and will end with an order, and in that order - and we have discussed a number of examples yesterday evening and this morning - the subordination is specified in detail. The commander will not only explain what the mission will be and where the mission will be carried out, but also which units will be involved and who will be in charge, who will be in command. This order here, the order we are discussing at the moment, does not relate to a specific operation but relates to the general situation. I.e., there can be operation -- excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it means that there is no specific operation taking place and as long as there is no specific operation taking place, then there is no need to subordinate, for example, police to the JNA. Of course, there will be negotiations, or there will be coordination, cooperation, between the JNA and local police if such a police exist. For example, in the situation when there was an operation aimed at seizing a particular area, when the mission has been accomplished and the area has been seized, then -- and when the JNA commander then knows that I can rely on the civilian police and civilian structures to maintain law and order, then there will be -- there will be negotiations and talks between these two bodies, in order to transfer authority. And this is what actually the order of Vukovic refers to. He's not referring specifically to crimes that are committed while operations are taking place. He mentions, for example, looting and I think harassment of the civilian population. That is something that also takes place once the particular operation is finished. Once a village has been captured, then the situation has to be normalised as soon as possible, and if there are civilian bodies, for authority and security, these bodies have to come into action following, of course, negotiations with the JNA command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have some questions but I would rather leave them at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise if I was not precise enough but I could -- for example, but maybe it brings us too far but you could, for example, link it to current situations. The conflict in Iraq, for example, once the military has achieved its goals, then you want civilian authority, if such a civilian authority exists, to take over as soon as possible. But, of course, the requirement is that the civilian authority exists and it's just not that somebody declares, "I'm the civilian authority and I take over." No, this is part of a process, and there are negotiations and there are -- there will maybe be an agreement about who will be responsible for what, in order to share the burden, for example, between military police and civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I have an objection, Your Honour. They are now giving for an example a situation that has nothing to do with the actual one, either in factual or in legal sense. In Iraq, they have foreign troops, whereas the JNA was a legal federal armed force in its own territory. Could we be please given an actual, real life situation? This is the gist of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it was offered just as an illustration, but I think we can move on to some other questions and hopefully -- either I'll clarify it or Your Honour will have, of course, the chance to ask more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure we can clarify this by sticking to the facts of the case, Mr. Theunens. The question that I did want to ask, which I was reluctant to ask, was I do understand what you say, the transitional period of the military handing over to civilian authority. But my understanding, and this is a very ignorant understanding because I have no knowledge of military issues, but from what we have been saying, I would expect that up until some order comes from within the military, some commander, to say military operations have now ceased, we hand over to civilian society, the military would be in control. And the military would maintain discipline, even of the armed forces who are not in operation but are just generally in control of the area to make sure that there is law and order, and if they start looting, that they are going to be disciplined by a military court, not a civilian court, even at that stage. I would therefore expect that there would be a very clear point in time when authority would be transferred to the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I in this connection ask if I understand correctly that in paragraphs 5 and 6, the military court is being addressed, in fact, but in connection with the prosecutor's office from Zagreb, as it says in point 6, with its seat in Banja Luka? Does this have any specific meaning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I would first like to answer to the first question, Your Honours. It is, of course, correct that a handover can only take place on orders. So this order we are discussing now does not allow to conclude when a handover has taken place. The order in -- at the end of the second paragraph only mentions that there are bodies of civilian authority that are, according to the commander, able to maintain law and order and also to act against crimes, crimes committed in first instance by civilians, because, to answer to the second question, it is correct when we look at the regulations that apply to military court and military prosecutors, which are discussed in the first section of my report, military courts and military prosecutors will take care of crimes allegedly committed by military personnel, but it could be that there were others involved. And that, for example, applies to if there are volunteers involved, or policemen. It will depend of the investigation and also the cooperation between the military court and the civilian court - we have to see whether there is a civilian court at that time in Knin that is operating - to see who will be in charge of prosecuting and then trying non-military personnel who have been involved in crimes. But, of course, before such a thing can take place, there have to be arrangements for handover of power in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, in terms of -- and please explain if I'm misunderstanding you. I've understood the explanation thus far from your report that anybody - volunteer or policeman - who acts as a soldier for any reason, resists any attack, becomes part of the armed forces and becomes subject to the military court discipline. Therefore, whether you're a policeman or a volunteer, if you have volunteered into the military, you are subject to discipline by the military and not by the civilian court for as long as cessation of hostilities has not been ordered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is indeed correct that according to the All People's Defence Law anybody who takes up weapons and participate in the defence of the country will be considered a member of the armed forces. However, I would like to make one observation: That is that, as is also mentioned in the first section of the report, at a certain moment we see the appearance of what is called or what are called volunteer groups. These are actually paramilitary formations who mainly pursue political goals, and for the groups originating from Serbia, they pursued purely Serbian goals, also known as the achievement of a Greater Serbia. When doing research for my report for the Milosevic case, we had, for example, a series of documents related to crimes in an area and I believe these were crimes in Western Slavonia, if I recall well, and we had a report from a security organ who said, well, crimes have taken place there, he informs his superior, the military prosecutor is being informed, then we see an exchange of reports between various military prosecutors, and then also the information is forwarded to a civilian prosecutor in Novi Sad in Serbia because the military prosecutor says, well, these were not military personnel; i.e., these were members of a volunteer group, and therefore we are not competent for these people. Now, I can only explain to you what I've seen in the documents, and like you, I notice that there is a discrepancy between what was stated in the de jure regulations, like the law for the military prosecutor and for military courts on one hand, and on the other hand, the enforcement of discipline and military justice on - in this case - volunteers. For the police are concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But we are actually not even sure that this paragraph relates to volunteers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, but I wanted to give an introduction to my reply to say, well, like the first category of volunteers where on one hand, according to the law, they should be at all times subject to military discipline and also military justice should apply to them. We see that in practice there has at least been one exception. When talking now about police, I have to mention that I didn't study the police discipline or police justice structures and regulations that apply to that because that was outside the scope of my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, but if police participate in military action, they can forget about the police disciplinary code. They then become subject to military disciplinary court; isn't that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the operations, yes, and it would seem logical that the first person who informs the military prosecutor about the crimes will be a military officer, will be the superior of these policemen or a soldier who participated in the operations. But then for the procedure to take place, I'm not in a position to answer the question. I don't know that -- based on the documents I reviewed, I cannot draw any conclusions on whether the military prosecutor should prosecute these people or they should be deferred to the procedures that are -- that apply to the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All we can say is probably what my very first question; this paragraph seems to go contrary to the de jure structure of discipline within the military as we understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can't explain. You were not there. You were not an eyewitness. You were an expert witness. All I'm saying, from -- is it fair to conclude or is it fair to infer from this paragraph that what this paragraph says goes contra to what ought to happen if we look at the law of the war of the country at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You wanted the document to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, I would, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted, and may it be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 59, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In an effort to clarify and not to confuse what we just talked about, Mr. Theunens, is there any distinction between who commands units in an operational group and who has jurisdiction to actually try those people who participated for any violations that are committed, or does command and disciplinary jurisdictions, are those permanently tied together or is there a distinction between those two?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, if I understand the question well, there is a distinction, and there should be a distinction because military discipline -- military justice, at least, should be independent. In the military, distinction is made between military discipline and military justice. Military discipline applies to minor violations; for example, of somebody who is late or who fails to carry out the assignment within the right conditions or the right way as it was expected by the commander, and there, of course, the commander is most responsible. For what military justice is concerned, of course, the commander, like any other JNA officer, has the duty to report alleged violations of the laws and customs of war. He can also task people to carry out an investigation. However, the traditional procedure based on the doctrine would be that the commander informs security organs or the military police, they will carry out the investigation, and then the information related to the investigation is forwarded through these channels - so the security organs or military police channels - to the competent authorities and that will be, in first instance, the military prosecutor, in order to avoid, for example, interference from the commander with the justice system.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you know the answer to this, would it be possible for that investigation process to result in a referral to some other body other than the military justice organs?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the documents I mentioned earlier, documents I reviewed for the Milosevic case that were related to crimes in Western Slavonia, the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What would the answer be in relation to this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my report on the pages -- on page 118, at the top, I have discussed a number of documents which are reports from security organs and a military police officer about crimes that have been committed in Skabrnja, which is located west of Knin, on the 18th of November 1991. Before addressing these documents, I would like to draw your attention on the previous page in my report, page 117 in the English version, where, in the second -- where in paragraph under the heading 2, Skabrnja-Nadin, we see that on the 20th of November, the Naval Military District, which is the most senior JNA command structure in the area, and which is also the superior command echelon to the 9th Corps, is informed by ECMM, so the European -- at that time called the European Community Monitoring Mission, about information the ECMM has received from the Croatian side about, I quote, "... a crime against 30 people, who were slaughtered ... in Skabrnja." ECMM asks the Naval Military District to have access to the area of Skabrnja. This is refused. But the Naval Military District then asks the 9th Corps to provide a report on the situation in Skabrnja, what has happened, because Skabrnja is located in the zone of responsibility of the 9th Corps. Now, the documents I have discussed right here, the ECMM request, that was a document I found myself doing a document search mission in the Croatian state archives, and unfortunately we couldn't find the response of the 9th Corps in the collection. Some documents were missing. So I'm not in a position to say whether the 9th Corps, which had been tasked by its superior command, investigated the crime. Now, all we have are reports which were compiled somewhat later in November and until March 1992, by security organs, mentioned on page 118 of my report, about those crimes. And we don't have any follow-up documents. I don't know -- I'm not in a position to say whether any measures were taken based on the investigation of the security organs who clearly identify the alleged perpetrators. They mention that, "the killings had been committed by members of the Benkovac Territorial Defence Staff special units or units that fought under their command." There was mentioning of a group called Opacic, but again, I don't know what happened, I'm not in a position to say what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You certainly wouldn't be in a position to say, sir, but I would offer this comment: The situation that you're now talking about seems to be distinguishable from the situation that we are talking about. Here, you're having the ECMM making an inquiry, and you can see the military wants to protect itself, doesn't want to give ECMM carte blanche to find out what happened. They say no, no, no, no, you don't come in, we'll investigate, we'll tell you, and then you don't get the report. That situation is distinguishable from a situation where the military itself believes that some of its members have committed a crime and have to discipline them. I don't know whether this is what you are envisaging, Mr. Black, in your question, and I do realise that we have gone past, yes, but I would like to wrap up this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. If I could try to ask one or two questions, I think hopefully we'll wrap it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, do you know in this scenario we have been discussing where, for example, police units are subordinated to a JNA commander for an operation, do you know what responsibility or what recourse the police commander of those units would have available to him? Would he have any recourse for alleged violations that occurred during the operations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the purely common sense point of view I would assume yes, but again, this report is limited to military aspects, so I'm not really in a position to give an authoritative answer into what a police commander could or should or may have done, so I prefer not to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. Just one thing to clarify to make sure we responded to the Chamber's questions: The prosecutor's office from Zagreb, is that a military or a civilian prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a military prosecutor's office at the time in Zagreb but, of course, due to the events, the evolution of the situation in Croatia, that military prosecutor office had to be moved to let's call it less hostile territory, and that could explain why reference is made to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Where is Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banja Luka is located in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to look at the document that you mentioned, which is referred to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it still on the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, I was going to move on to the next point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's about time, I think -- or wouldn't that be a convenient time? We should have gone at quarter to. Am I right? I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think we have until 10.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is a document that was mentioned at page 118 of the report, which I think is page 138 or 139 of the B/C/S. The 65 ter number is 2065, and the B/C/S ERN number is 04144389. Mr. Theunens, is this the document that you were referring to earlier, that you see on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. This is the Naval Military District, which was the superior command of the 9th Corps, forwarding the request of the EC Mission to the 9th Corps. And again it shows that Skabrnja is located within the zone of responsibility of the 9th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, rather than repeat what he said before, could this receive a number and be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, there is one last major topic within section 3 of the report, and that's the establishment of the RSK TO and its transformation into, "special police brigades." This begins at page 118 of your report, in fact at page 140 in the B/C/S. My first question for you, you talk about the Vance Plan. What was the Vance Plan, how did it come about, and what were its provisions?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 23rd of November 1991, the president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, president of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, and the federal secretary for people's defence, army General Veljko Kadijevic signed a cease-fire agreement in Geneva, and this cease-fire agreement was the precursor of the Vance Plan, which was agreed upon by the same people on the 2nd of January 1992. The Vance Plan consists of three phases: The first phase was the deployment of a UN, so blue helmet, peace force in a number of areas in Croatia, which were called UNPAs, United Nations Protected Areas. The UNPAs were areas in Croatia where, according to the Secretary-General of the United Nations, special arrangements were needed to maintain peace and security. These were areas where already before the conflict or due to the conflict, as a result of the conflict, there was a significant presence of Serbs; majority or significant minority. The second phase of the plan consisted of demilitarisation. Demilitarisation implied withdrawal of the JNA and the Croatian forces, which then had the name HV, as well as the demobilisation, disbanding and disarmament of the local Serb TO. The weapons of the TO would then be stored in what was called a dual key, under dual key system in warehouses. Dual key meant there was a key held by UN peace forces, UNPROFOR, and SAO Krajina or local Serb TO. The SAO Krajina or the local Serbs were allowed to maintain a lightly armed police force and this police force would be monitored by UN police. And the third phase, then, of the Vance Plan consisted of the maintaining of peace and security to allow the return of refugees of all ethnic origins. Now, overall, the Vance Plan, it was always insisted in Security Council resolutions and related reports that it was just an interim arrangement, and that was one of the problems with the implementation of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What is the time line of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any specific time line. The resolution that allowed the deployment of the entire peace force provided UNPROFOR an initial mandate of one year. However, in this resolution, it was also insisted, as I mentioned, that it wasn't -- the Vance Plan was intended as an interim arrangement aimed at creating conditions of peace and security and global conditions to allow negotiations on a political solution. So the Vance Plan in no way precluded or preempted a political solution to the conflict. And if I may, this was actually one of the problems because the two main parties involved, Croatia and the Serbs in the SAO Krajina, which in the meanwhile had become the RSK, had a totally different interpretation. Croatia basically saw the Vance Plan as a very short term arrangement and was mindful of situations like Cyprus; i.e., didn't want the UN presence to last, whereas the Serbs in the Krajina, in the RSK, considered the Vance Plan as a confirmation or consolidation of the existence of their own entity at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'm going to ask you some questions now about what you told us. Could you look at page 120 of your report, please. That's page 141 of the B/C/S. There is a map there and, Your Honours, this was one of the colour pages that I handed out yesterday. You can see that map much more clearly on the colour handout. Mr. Theunens, could you tell us what's depicted here on this map on page 120.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map on page 120, I found it in documents available to the OTP. From the language, it can be concluded that this is a document, that the map has been produced by the authorities of the entity known as the RSK, and it depicts the United Nations Protected Areas together with areas also known as pink zones. Maybe I should first explain the legend.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though in B/C/S it's clear, but number 1 refers to the part of Western Slavonia which was outside -- where there was no permanent UNPROFOR presence. So it was basically part of Western Slavonia with a significant presence of Serbs but where there was no permanent presence of UN blue helmets, because the UN blue helmets had only a permanent presence within the UNPAs, but the blue helmets would patrol these areas. Number 2 refers to an area known as the Miljevac or Miljevci - I've seen the two spellings - plateau. This was an area which was, based on the information I reviewed, not located in the UNPA itself but in the pink zone. Pink zones were areas outside the UNPAs where there was a significant presence of Serbs. Now, how come that there were pink zones? The problem was that the borders of the UNPAs had been negotiated between November and let's say January 1992. In some areas, the fighting continued. Now, Croatia wanted to have the UNPAs as small as possible. I'm a bit exaggerating but that's more or less how it was, because basically these UNPAs were part of the Croatian territory where the Croatian authorities had no authority. On the other hand, the Serb side wanted to have the UNPAs as large as possible, because the more territory you control, the more powerful you are. Now, a compromise was found, boundaries for the UNPAs were established, but nevertheless when the UN peace forces started to deploy, and that was around April 1992, it was -- the situation was such that there was a significant Serb presence outside the UNPAs, so outside the areas where the UNPROFOR forces were mandated to be deployed, and actually without protection. So that's why pink zones were defined. These were, as I mentioned, areas outside the UNPAs with a significant Serb presence, where there was no permanent presence of UNPROFOR, where UNPROFOR would patrol. So number 2 on the map, Miljevac plateau. Number 3 refers to the area of Maslenica. Number 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There are two number 3s. Are there two Maslenicas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you're correct, Your Honour. I didn't see it there. The number 3 on the right side, so in the southeast, refers to Peruca, the area of the Peruca dam; and the number 3 on the left side refers to the area of the Maslenica bridge as it existed prior to the conflict. Number 4 refers to the area of the Medak. And as I mentioned, this bridge -- this map comes from an RSK source. The areas 3 -- excuse me, 2, 3 -- I mean the two 3s and number 4 are areas where Croatian forces carried out operations between June 1992 and September 1993. The Croatian military launched an operation in the Miljevac or Miljevci plateau in June 1992. Similar events happened in the area of Maslenica and Peruca in January 1993. And then to conclude, there was also a Croatian military operation incursion in the area known as the Medak pocket in September 1993. The other numbers, number 5 indicates in Western Slavonia, the area -- the part of Western Slavonia where UNPROFOR was deployed. Number 6 refers to Sector South. And number 7 refers to Baranja and Eastern Slavonia, which was also known as Sector East. And I didn't mention Western Slavonia is Sector West. And then the northern part of the -- is it of the blue area was known as Sector North in the UN documents, UNPROFOR documents. So there were three UNPAs covering four sectors, and together with the UNPAs there were also a number of pink zones, three of them we have discussed here with the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you say that in the largest UNPA here there were two sectors. Do you know more approximately where the border was between those two sectors?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you look on the map, you see Bihac mentioned in the white area just left of the legend. The limit between Sector North and Sector South would more or less be a horizontal line just south of Bihac but then within the blue area. But these were mainly technical boundaries purely for the use by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is just for sort of Your Honour's knowledge. I could have him mark this but I hadn't planned to do it but I want to make sure that it's clear. Would you like him to mark that on the map? Or is it necessary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe let's mark it now that it has at least been referred to in evidence specifically. Shall we then admit it formally into evidence? And I know it is admitted already, but can we give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may be an appropriate time to try for the first time the marking on e-court. We could pull this page of his report up on e-court and theoretically he can mark it straight on there, it can be saved and made an exhibit electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it could probably be marked 6A or 6 something because it is part of Exhibit 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's go for the exercise on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is page 120 of the English. I hope that it's in colour in e-court. It's actually something I don't know, Your Honour. If it's not in colour, we can do it the old-fashioned way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can tell you, the old-fashioned way always works.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's the great thing about the old-fashioned way. If I can assist, perhaps, the Court officer and usher, we will need to see the English version, and the pagination is ever so slightly different. It may be about page 140 -- in terms of e-court pagination - I don't want to confuse the issue - on the hard copy of the report it's marked at page 120. Your Honour, why don't we go ahead and do it the old-fashioned way. I can discuss with the registry to make sure we are on the same page for the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's do it the old-fashioned way then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, if I could pass this to the witness and have him put it on the ELMO it might be the best operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I could make sure that the audiovisual booth is giving us the ELMO on its channel. Sometimes, Your Honour, even the old-fashioned way has its problems. Is it on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The very old, old-fashioned way, where you do it on hard copy by hand. It looks like we've got a technical problem with the audiovisual people outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK

utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, if could you take that map on page 120 that we have been discussing and just draw with your pen the line of demarcation approximately between the two sectors.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to emphasise it's an approximate line because the map is very small. It was only for technical use within UNPROFOR because this was all part of a zone which was subject to the same mandate, so it's just to separate the zones of the various commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, then if that could be made an exhibit and given a number, admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we -- did we agree that we are going to make it a subset of 6 or do you want a new number completely?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: However Your Honour prefers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, at pages 100 and 121 of your report, which are pages 142 to 143 in B/C/S, you discuss the creation of the Republika Srpska Krajina, or the RSK, which in English translates essentially as Serbian Republic of Krajina. When was the RSK established?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: RSK as such -- the constitution for the RSK, if I recall, was adopted in December 1991. But because I didn't discuss it really on my document, I mainly focussed on the military aspects, but then the other parties; i.e., we had an SAO Serbian Krajina which we have been discussing extensively for the 1991 events, then there was also an SAO Western Slavonia and an SAO Baranja, Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem, they joined the SAO Krajina, resulting in the RSK, and I believe that process took place in the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You note on page 122 of your report that the new RSK constitution defined armed forces. What definition did they give?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, the armed forces, according to Article 102 of the January 1992 RSK constitution, the Territorial Defence of the RSK were the armed forces of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was that consistent with the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Vance Plan stipulated, the disarming, disbanding and demobilising of the TO, of course, there is no problem having a constitution as long as these armed forces are not activated, and abide by the conditions imposed by the Vance Plan, but as is discussed further on in the report, actually, this aspect of the constitution was also put into practice, so the bringing into practice would, for my view, represent a violation of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You mentioned three phases of the Vance Plan. Which part specifically would this be in conflict with?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is specifically in conflict with the second phase because there clearly, according to this phase, the RSK was only allowed to maintain a lightly armed police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to start a new subtopic. Perhaps it's a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it's a convenient time, then maybe we can take a break. We will come back at quarter to 11. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Black, just a housekeeping issue. It has come to the Chamber's notice that the courtroom is available for the rest of today. utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree, Your Honour, yes.
